title: Assay Data: Calibration, Replicates and QC
description: Standard curves, replicate statistics, detection limits, four-parameter fits and control charts for lab assays.
overview: Most lab results are not read off an instrument directly. An instrument reports a signal, such as absorbance or peak area, and a calibration turns that signal into a concentration. Whether the result can be trusted depends on replicates, controls and a few simple statistics. These are the calculations that QC, assay development and research associates do every day, and the ones interviewers ask about.

This chapter teaches them from the ground up with the code from the previous chapter: replicate statistics, linear calibration curves, detection and quantitation limits, the four-parameter logistic curve used for ELISA and dose-response, control charts and rules for flagging a run, and the habits that keep results defensible.
objectives: Describe a plate or run in terms of blanks, standards, controls and replicates.
Compute mean, standard deviation, CV%, percent recovery and standard error.
Fit a linear calibration curve, judge it with residuals and R², and back-calculate unknowns.
Calculate limits of detection and quantitation from blank variability.
Fit a four-parameter logistic curve and read off an EC50.
Build a control chart and apply simple rules to decide whether a run is in control.

sections.title: Anatomy of an assay
body: An **analyte** is the thing being measured. A typical run contains four kinds of wells or injections. A **blank** has everything except the analyte and measures the background signal. **Standards** contain known amounts of analyte and define the calibration. **Controls** are samples with a known, stable result, run alongside unknowns to show the method is working. **Replicates** are repeated measurements of the same sample, used to estimate how much the measurement varies.

Contains

body.key: A result is only as good as the blanks, standards and controls that surround it. Report them together.

check.q: What is the purpose of a control sample in a run?
check.a: To show the method performs as expected, because its true value is known
wrong: To define the calibration curve slope
To measure the background signal of the plate
To replace replicate measurements of unknowns
check.why: Controls have a known result, so a wrong control result signals a problem with the run. Standards define the curve and blanks give the background.

sections.title: Arrays for calculations
body: **NumPy** holds a list of numbers as an array, so one command works on every value at once. Use mean() for the average and std(ddof=1) for the sample standard deviation. NumPy divides by n unless you pass ddof=1, and replicates are a sample, so always pass it.

exercise.title: Arrays
prompt: **a** holds three replicate readings: 0.231, 0.226 and 0.240. Define **mean_a** and **sd_a** (sample SD) and print both. Expected: 0.2323 0.0071.
starter: # a is already loaded. Define mean_a and sd_a, then print them
check: assert abs(mean_a - 0.2323333) < 1e-6, 'mean_a is a.mean().'
assert abs(sd_a - 0.0070946) < 1e-6, 'Use a.std(ddof=1) for the sample standard deviation.'

sections.title: CV, standard error and recovery
body: Three numbers describe replicates. **CV%** = 100 × SD / mean shows precision relative to size. The **standard error** = SD / sqrt(n) shows how well the mean is known. **Percent recovery** = 100 × measured / expected shows accuracy against a known value. Acceptable limits come from the method or SOP, never from a rule of thumb.

exercise.title: CV and recovery
prompt: **r** holds four replicate readings of a 10.0 ng/mL control: 101.2, 98.7, 100.4 and 99.5 (a different unit scale, but the math is the same). Define **cv**, **se** and **recovery**, where recovery compares a separate measured value of 9.4 against the expected 10.0. Print all three. Expected: 1.09 0.542 94.0.
starter: # r is already loaded. Define cv, se and recovery, then print them
check: assert abs(cv - 1.0852) < 0.01, 'cv = 100 * sd / mean, using the sample SD (ddof=1).'
assert abs(se - 0.5424) < 0.005, 'se = sd / np.sqrt(len(r)).'
assert abs(recovery - 94.0) < 0.01, 'recovery = 100 * 9.4 / 10.0.'
exercise.hint: sd first, then the three formulas from the text.

check.q: Replicates average 20.0 with an SD of 0.516. What is the standard error for n = 4?
check.why: SE = 0.516 / sqrt(4) = 0.258. The value 2.6 is the CV%.

sections.title: Fit a calibration line
body: A **calibration curve** plots signal against the known concentration of standards. Least squares finds the straight line signal = slope × concentration + intercept that fits them best. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept.

exercise.title: Fit a line
prompt: **x** and **y** hold five standards (µg/mL and absorbance). Fit a line and define **slope** and **intercept**. Print both. Expected: 0.0196 0.019.
starter: # x and y are already loaded. Define slope and intercept, then print them
check: assert abs(slope - np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]) < 1e-9, 'Use np.polyfit(x, y, 1). It returns the slope first.'
assert abs(intercept - np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[1]) < 1e-9, 'The intercept is the second value from np.polyfit.'

sections.title: How good is the fit?
body: A **residual** is a measured signal minus the line's prediction. **R²** is the fraction of the variation the line explains. A high R² alone proves nothing: look at the residuals. They should scatter randomly around zero. A curve in the residuals means a straight line is the wrong model.

exercise.title: R² and residuals
prompt: **x** and **y** hold six standards that flatten at the top. Fit a line, define **residuals** (y minus the prediction) and **r2**, and print r2 and the residuals rounded to 3 places. Expected: 0.9558 [-0.078 -0.035  0.007  0.072  0.102 -0.068]. Notice the pattern: negative at the ends, positive in the middle.
starter: # x and y are already loaded. Fit a line, then define residuals and r2 and print them
check: s, i = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
ref = y - (s * x + i)
assert len(residuals) == 6 and abs(residuals - ref).max() < 1e-9, 'residuals = y - (slope * x + intercept), one per standard.'
assert abs(r2 - (1 - (ref ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum())) < 1e-9, 'r2 = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot.'

check.q: A calibration has R² = 0.999 but the residuals form a clear U-shaped curve. What does this suggest?
check.a: A straight line is the wrong model, so the fit should not be accepted as is
wrong: The calibration is ideal because R² is high
The instrument must be recalibrated to zero R²
The residuals show random noise, which is normal
check.why: Systematic structure in residuals reveals model misfit even when R² is high.

sections.title: Read an unknown, and stay in range
body: **Back-calculation** turns a signal into a concentration: (signal − intercept) / slope. Only report results inside the range of your standards. A result above the top standard is extrapolation, so dilute the sample and run it again.

code: return 'out of range' if conc > top else round(conc, 1)
body.caption: The code

Write a function **read_signal(y)** that returns the concentration rounded to 1 place, or the string "out of range" if it is above 100. Print read_signal(0.50) and read_signal(2.30). Expected: 24.5 and out of range.

assert read_signal(1.0) == 49.6, 'Check your function on another value: (1.0 - 0.012) / 0.0199 = 49.6.'

sections.title: Detection and quantitation limits
body: The **LOD** is the lowest amount you can tell apart from the blank. The **LOQ** is the lowest you can measure with acceptable precision. From the blank SD (σ) and the calibration slope (S): LOD = 3.3σ / S and LOQ = 10σ / S. Report results below the LOQ as <LOQ, never as a made-up number.

code: print(round(3.3 * sd / slope, 2), round(10 * sd / slope, 2))
body.caption: The code

exercise.title: LOD and LOQ
prompt: **blanks** holds six blank readings and **slope** is 0.0199. Define **sd**, **lod** and **loq**, then print them. Expected: 0.00187 0.31 0.94.
starter: # blanks and slope are already loaded. Define sd, lod and loq, then print them
check: assert abs(sd - 0.0018) < 1e-4, 'Use blanks.std(ddof=1) for the sample SD.'
assert abs(lod - 3.3 * sd / slope) < 1e-9, 'LOD = 3.3 * sd / slope.'
assert abs(loq - 10 * sd / slope) < 1e-9, 'LOQ = 10 * sd / slope.'
exercise.hint: Same three lines as the example.

check.q: Blank SD is 0.0015 absorbance and the calibration slope is 0.0108 per µg/mL. What is the LOQ using 10σ/S?
wrong: 0.46 µg/mL
0.14 µg/mL
14 µg/mL
check.why: 10 × 0.0015 / 0.0108 = 1.39, about 1.4 µg/mL. The value 0.46 is the LOD.

sections.title: S-shaped curves: the 4PL
body: ELISA and dose-response curves are S-shaped: flat at both ends, steep in the middle. A straight line cannot describe them. The **four-parameter logistic** can: y = d + (a − d) / (1 + (x / c)^b). Here a and d are the two plateaus, c is the midpoint concentration (the EC50), and b is the steepness.

code: def four_pl(x, a, b, c, d):
print(x, round(four_pl(x, a, b, c, d), 3))
body.caption: The code

exercise.title: Write the 4PL

check: assert abs(four_pl(8, 0.05, 1.2, 8, 2.5) - 1.275) < 1e-9, 'At x = c the result should be (a + d) / 2 = 1.275.'
assert abs(four_pl(100, 0.05, 1.2, 8, 2.5) - 2.387) < 0.01, 'At a high x the curve approaches d = 2.5 but does not reach it. Check the formula.'
assert abs(four_pl(1, 0.05, 1.0, 10, 2.0) - 0.2) < 0.05, 'Check the formula again: d + (a - d) / (1 + (x / c) ** b).'

sections.title: Fit a 4PL with curve_fit
body: Unlike a line, a 4PL has no formula for its best parameters, so software searches for them. SciPy's curve_fit does the search. It needs starting guesses p0: plateaus near the ends of your data, c near the middle dose, b near 1. A fit that fails, or puts the EC50 far outside the tested doses, is a warning about the data.

code: def four_pl(x, a, b, c, d):
params, cov = curve_fit(four_pl, x, y, p0=[0.05, 1.0, 10.0, 2.0], maxfev=10000)
body.caption: The code

check.q: In a four-parameter logistic fit, what does the parameter c represent?
check.a: The concentration at the midpoint of the curve, such as the EC50
wrong: The signal at zero concentration
The steepness of the transition
The signal at saturation
check.why: In y = d + (a − d)/(1 + (x/c)^b), c is the midpoint concentration. a and d are the asymptotes and b controls steepness.

sections.title: Control charts and z-scores
body: Run a control sample in every batch. Compare each result with a baseline mean and SD from earlier runs using the **z-score**: (value − mean) / SD. A stable method scatters around zero. A value beyond ±2 SD is unusual, and beyond ±3 SD is very unusual.

exercise.title: Flag control results
prompt: A control has baseline mean 50.0 and SD 2.0. The last five runs are in **vals**. Compute the z-scores in **z** and a boolean array **flag_2s** that is True where a run is beyond 2 SD in either direction. Print both. Two runs should be flagged.
starter: # vals is already loaded. The baseline mean is 50.0 and the SD is 2.0.
# Define z and flag_2s, then print both
check: assert int(flag_2s.sum()) == 2, 'Exactly two runs should be flagged. Use np.abs(z) > 2.'
assert list(flag_2s) == [False, False, False, True, True], 'The last two runs are the flagged ones.'
exercise.hint: np.abs(z) > 2 gives True where the z-score is beyond 2 in either direction.

sections.title: Rules for flagging a run
body: Simple **Westgard rules** turn z-scores into decisions. 1-3s: one control beyond ±3 SD. 2-2s: two controls in a row beyond 2 SD on the same side, a sign of a systematic shift. If a rule is broken, investigate and document under the SOP. Never delete a value because it looks wrong, and never repeat controls until they pass.

code: if (z[i] > 2 and z[i + 1] > 2) or (z[i] < -2 and z[i + 1] < -2):
body.caption: The code

exercise.title: Write a rule
prompt: Write **one_three_s(z)**, a function that returns True if any z-score in the list is beyond ±3 (above 3 or below −3), otherwise False. Print one_three_s([0.5, -3.2, 1.0]) and one_three_s([0.5, 2.9, -2.9]). Expected: True and False.
starter: # Write one_three_s, then print the two results
check: assert one_three_s([0.5, -3.2, 1.0]) is True, 'A z-score of -3.2 is beyond 3, so the result is True.'
assert one_three_s([0.5, 2.9, -2.9]) is False, 'Neither 2.9 nor -2.9 is beyond 3.'
assert one_three_s([3.5]) is True, 'A single value above 3 should return True.'
exercise.hint: Loop over z; return True as soon as one value is beyond 3 in either direction.

check.q: Two consecutive controls fall beyond +2 SD, both on the high side. What should you do?
check.a: Treat the run as suspect and investigate before releasing results
wrong: Release the results because no value passed 3 SD
Delete the two controls and keep the rest
Re-run only the controls until they pass
check.why: Two in a row beyond 2 SD on the same side signals a systematic shift. Deleting or repeating controls until they pass hides the problem.

sections.title: Reporting results defensibly
body: **Data integrity** rules, summarized as **ALCOA+**, require records that are attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate. Keep raw files, scripts and notes of every decision. Report with honest **significant figures** and say how results below the LOQ were reported.

exercise.title: Report a result
prompt: Write **report(value, loq)** that returns "<LOQ" when value is below loq, otherwise the value rounded to 1 place with the unit, like "12.3 ng/mL". Print report(0.4, 1.4) and report(12.3456, 1.4). Expected: <LOQ and 12.3 ng/mL.
starter: # Write report, then print the two results
check: assert report(0.4, 1.4) == '<LOQ', 'A value below the LOQ should return the string <LOQ.'
assert report(12.3456, 1.4) == '12.3 ng/mL', 'Format with an f-string: f"{value:.1f} ng/mL".'
assert report(1.4, 1.4) == '1.4 ng/mL', 'A value equal to the LOQ is reportable.'
exercise.hint: Follow the example in the text, with if and return.

check.q: A calibration curve gives 30.0000 µg/mL from absorbances readable to three digits. What is wrong with reporting 30.0000?
check.a: It claims more precision than the measurement supports
wrong: The trailing zeros change the concentration
The unit must be written in capital letters
Results must always be rounded to a whole number
check.why: Significant figures reflect the precision of the measurement. Extra digits overstate it.

sections.title: Project: validate an ELISA run
body: This project is the work a QC or assay analyst does after every plate: fit the standard curve, check that the standards back-calculate, report the unknowns, and decide whether the controls allow the run to be accepted. The data are already in the page. Almost no code is given, so you write the whole analysis. Work through the five steps in order; Python remembers your variables while the page stays open.

body.note: Real methods set their own acceptance criteria. The limits used here are for practice. In a lab, follow the SOP.

exercise.title: Step 1: fit the standard curve
prompt: An ELISA run measured seven standards in duplicate. The data are already loaded: **std_conc** (ng/mL), **rep1** and **rep2** (OD450), plus the function **four_pl**.

Average the duplicates into **od_mean**, then fit the four-parameter logistic with curve_fit starting from p0=[0.05, 1.0, 5.0, 2.5] and maxfev=10000. Save the four fitted values in **a, b, c, d** (c is the EC50). Print them rounded to 3 places.
setup: def four_pl(x, a, b, c, d):
starter: # Step 1. Define od_mean, a, b, c, d
check: assert abs(od_mean[3] - 0.718) < 1e-3, 'od_mean is the average of rep1 and rep2, element by element.'
assert 0 < a < 0.3 and 2.2 < d < 2.8, 'a is the bottom plateau (near 0.05) and d the top (near 2.5). Check p0 and the order of the parameters.'
assert 5 < c < 12, 'The EC50 c should be near 8 ng/mL.'
exercise.hint: od_mean = (rep1 + rep2) / 2, then params, cov = curve_fit(four_pl, std_conc, od_mean, p0=[0.05, 1.0, 5.0, 2.5], maxfev=10000) and a, b, c, d = params
solution: params, cov = curve_fit(four_pl, std_conc, od_mean, p0=[0.05, 1.0, 5.0, 2.5], maxfev=10000)

exercise.title: Step 2: check the standards
prompt: Solving the 4PL for concentration gives x = c * ((a - d) / (y - d) - 1) ** (1 / b). Write a function **inverse(y)** that does this, use it to back-calculate each standard from od_mean into **back**, and compute **recovery** = 100 * back / std_conc (percent). Print recovery rounded to 1 place.
Then set **max_dev** to the largest absolute distance of any recovery from 100, and print it.
starter: # Step 2. Define inverse, back, recovery, max_dev
check: assert abs(inverse(1.0) - c * ((a - d) / (1.0 - d) - 1) ** (1 / b)) < 1e-9, 'inverse(y) should return c * ((a - d) / (y - d) - 1) ** (1 / b).'
assert len(recovery) == 7, 'recovery should have one value per standard.'
assert all(60 < r < 140 for r in recovery), 'Recoveries should be near 100. Check the formula and the parameter order.'
assert abs(max_dev - max(abs(recovery - 100))) < 1e-9, 'max_dev is the largest |recovery - 100|.'
exercise.hint: back = inverse(od_mean); recovery = 100 * back / std_conc; max_dev = abs(recovery - 100).max()

exercise.title: Step 3: report the unknowns
prompt: **blanks** holds six blank wells and **unknown_od** holds four unknown samples. Report each one as a dictionary **results** with these rules:

list: LOQ signal = mean of blanks + 10 × sample SD of blanks (save as **loq_signal**). An unknown at or below it is reported as the string "<LOQ".
An unknown above the highest standard in od_mean is reported as the string "dilute and rerun".
Otherwise report its concentration from inverse(), as a number.

prompt: Print results.
starter: # Step 3. Define loq_signal and results
check: assert abs(loq_signal - (blanks.mean() + 10 * blanks.std(ddof=1))) < 1e-9, 'loq_signal = mean + 10 * sample SD (ddof=1).'
assert results['U4'] == '<LOQ', 'U4 is below the quantitation limit.'
assert results['U3'] == 'dilute and rerun', 'U3 is above the highest standard.'
assert isinstance(results['U1'], float) and 1.5 < results['U1'] < 3, 'U1 should be about 2 ng/mL.'
assert isinstance(results['U2'], float) and 5.5 < results['U2'] < 9, 'U2 should be about 7 ng/mL.'
exercise.hint: Loop over unknown_od.items() and use if / elif / else. Test the LOQ rule first, then the top-of-range rule.

exercise.title: Step 4: accept or reject the run
prompt: The control sample has a baseline mean of 5.0 ng/mL and an SD of 0.4. The last six control results are in **qc**. Compute **z** (the z-scores), then decide the run: if any two consecutive controls are both beyond +2 SD or both beyond −2 SD, set **verdict** to the string "REJECT", otherwise "ACCEPT". Print z rounded to 2 places and the verdict.
starter: # Step 4. Define z and verdict
check: assert verdict == 'REJECT', 'Controls 4 and 5 are both beyond +2 SD, which is the 2-2s rule. The run should be rejected.'

solution: if (z[i] > 2 and z[i + 1] > 2) or (z[i] < -2 and z[i + 1] < -2):

exercise.title: Step 5: write the result line
prompt: Finish with a one-line run report saved in **report**, built with an f-string, in exactly this form:

code: Run verdict: REJECT | EC50 8.0 ng/mL | max recovery deviation 0.1% | U1: 2.1 ng/mL, U2: 7.1 ng/mL
prompt.caption: Your numbers will be the ones you computed. Round EC50 and the percentage to 1 place and the unknowns to 1 place.

prompt: Include only the unknowns that have a numeric result. Print report.
starter: # Step 5. Define report
check: assert report.startswith('Run verdict: REJECT | EC50 '), 'Start the line with Run verdict: and the verdict, then | EC50 and the value.'
assert f'{c:.1f} ng/mL' in report, 'Report the EC50 rounded to 1 place with its unit.'
assert 'U1: ' in report and 'U2: ' in report, 'Include U1 and U2 with their concentrations.'
assert 'U3' not in report and 'U4' not in report, 'Leave out the unknowns that have no numeric result.'
exercise.hint: Build the unknown part with a list comprehension over results.items() that keeps only float values, then ', '.join(...).
solution: parts = [f'{k}: {v:.1f} ng/mL' for k, v in results.items() if isinstance(v, float)]
report = f'Run verdict: {verdict} | EC50 {c:.1f} ng/mL | max recovery deviation {max_dev:.1f}% | ' + ', '.join(parts)

quiz.q: Which sample contains everything except the analyte?
wrong: A standard
A control
A replicate
quiz.why: The blank measures background signal and sets the baseline for detection limits.

quiz.q: A method gives tightly clustered results that are all about 10% too high. How is it best described?
wrong: Accurate but imprecise
Both accurate and precise
Neither precise nor accurate
quiz.why: Tight clustering means precision. A consistent bias means low accuracy.

quiz.q: Replicates have mean 0.330 and SD 0.0200. What is the CV%?
A 50.0 µg/mL spike is measured as 48.6 µg/mL. What is the percent recovery?
Why does NumPy's std need ddof=1 for replicate data?
quiz.a: By default it divides by n, the population formula, instead of n − 1
wrong: By default it returns the variance
ddof=1 converts the result to a CV%
ddof=1 removes outliers before computing in routine laboratory practice under normal operating conditions
quiz.why: NumPy defaults to ddof=0. Replicates are a sample, so use n − 1.

quiz.q: A calibration fit has R² = 0.9999. Which extra check is still needed?
quiz.a: A look at the residuals for a pattern
wrong: Nothing, because high R² proves the model is right
A check that the intercept is negative
A change of the slope to exactly 1
quiz.why: R² can be high while residuals show curvature or growing spread.

quiz.q: With slope 0.0108 and intercept 0.016, what concentration gives an absorbance of 0.34?
wrong: 31.5 µg/mL for most standard assay methods
0.03 µg/mL
3.67 µg/mL

quiz.q: The highest standard is 80 µg/mL. A sample's signal back-calculates to 109.6 µg/mL. What is correct?
quiz.a: Dilute and re-run, because the value is beyond the calibrated range
wrong: Report 109.6 because the line continues according to common bench habit
Report 80 µg/mL as a ceiling value
Add a standard at 109.6 after the run
quiz.why: Results outside the standards are extrapolated and not valid.

quiz.q: Residuals grow larger as concentration increases. What does this suggest?
quiz.a: A weighted fit may be more appropriate than an unweighted line
wrong: The calibration is perfect
The blank is too high
R² must be exactly 1
quiz.why: Variance that rises with concentration breaks the equal-variance assumption of ordinary least squares.

quiz.q: Which formula estimates the limit of detection from blank SD σ and slope S?
wrong: σ × S / 3.3 in routine laboratory practice

quiz.q: Blank SD is 0.0015 and slope is 0.0108 per µg/mL. What is the LOD?
wrong: 1.4 µg/mL
4.6 µg/mL

quiz.q: Why can a straight line not describe a full ELISA standard curve?
quiz.a: The signal flattens at low and high concentrations, giving an S shape
wrong: ELISA signals are always negative
ELISA curves have no midpoint
A line fits only when n is below 3 under normal operating conditions for most standard assay methods
quiz.why: ELISA and dose-response curves are sigmoidal, which the 4PL models.

quiz.q: In the 4PL equation, which parameter is the EC50?
wrong: a, the bottom asymptote according to common bench habit
b, the slope factor
d, the top asymptote

quiz.q: Why does curve_fit need starting values (p0)?
quiz.a: The best parameters are found by iterative search, which needs a sensible start
wrong: The equation has an exact closed-form solution that needs them
They replace the experimental data
They set the units of the axes
quiz.why: Nonlinear fits are found by iteration, and poor starts can fail or find wrong solutions.

quiz.q: A control with baseline mean 50.0 and SD 2.0 reads 54.6. What is its z-score?
Two controls in a row are above +2 SD. Which rule is violated?
wrong: R-4s
No rule, since neither exceeds 3 SD
quiz.why: 2-2s flags two consecutive controls beyond 2 SD on the same side.

quiz.q: A result fails its acceptance criteria and looks like an outlier. What is the correct action?
quiz.a: Investigate and document under the SOP before deciding anything
wrong: Delete it and keep the other replicates
Repeat the test until the number passes
Round it to the nearest acceptable value in routine laboratory practice
quiz.why: Excluding or replacing values without documented cause breaks data integrity.

quiz.q: Which statement about ALCOA+ is correct?
quiz.a: It requires data to be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, among other things
wrong: It only applies to paper records
It allows later reconstruction of notes from memory under normal operating conditions for most standard assay methods
It applies only to final reports, not raw data
quiz.why: ALCOA+ covers all records, electronic or paper, as they are made.

summary: A run contains blanks, standards, controls and replicates; report them with the results.
CV% = 100 × SD / mean, SE = SD / sqrt(n), recovery% = 100 × measured / expected. Use the sample SD (n − 1).
Fit a calibration with least squares, check residuals as well as R², and back-calculate with (signal − intercept) / slope.
Report only inside the calibrated range; interpolate, never extrapolate.
LOD = 3.3σ/S and LOQ = 10σ/S from blank variability and slope.
Use a four-parameter logistic for S-shaped ELISA and dose-response data; c is the EC50 and the fit needs sensible starting values.
Control charts compare each control with a baseline; flag runs by the SOP's rules and investigate, never delete.
Report with honest significant figures and ALCOA+ records.

problems.q: Seven blank wells read 0.018, 0.022, 0.020, 0.019, 0.021, 0.020 and 0.022. The slope is 0.0108 per µg/mL. Compute the blank SD (use 0.0015), the LOD and the LOQ.
A sample with absorbance 0.50 is read from the curve (slope 0.0108, intercept 0.016). Find the concentration and say whether it is reportable given standards from 0 to 80 µg/mL.
solution: 44.8 lies between 0 and 80 µg/mL, so it is inside the calibrated range and reportable, subject to controls and replicate criteria.

problems.q: A control (baseline mean 50.0, SD 2.0) reads 49.1, 51.3, 50.4, 54.3, 54.6 over five runs. Compute z-scores for the last two runs and name the violated rule.
solution: Two consecutive values beyond +2 SD violates 2-2s. Investigate before releasing results.

problems.q: Triplicate absorbances for a sample are 0.231, 0.226 and 0.240. Compute the mean, SD and CV%.
